Lusaka, Zambia – Zambia is attracting billions of dollars in mining investment as it seeks to become a significant supplier of minerals critical to the global energy transition. But as foreign companies expand operations and new projects come on stream, questions are mounting over whether common Zambians are benefitting from the country’s growing mineral wealth.
President Hakainde Hichilema said more than $12bn had been invested in Zambia’s mining sector since 2022, as the government pushes to increase copper production and attract new investors.
Leading investors include Canadian companies First Quantum Minerals and Barrick Mining Corporation, India’s Vedanta Resources and China Nonferrous Metal Mining Group (CNMC).
Abu Dhabi-based International Resources Holding (IRH) has also emerged as a leading investor after committing $1.1bn to recapitalise Mopani Copper Mines, previously owned by Glencore. The investment gave IRH a 51 percent stake in the mine, with state-owned ZCCM Investments Holdings retaining 49 percent.
Alongside large-scale mining projects, the Copperbelt province has also seen the expansion of smaller Chinese-owned mineral-processing plants, some sourcing ore from artisanal and small-scale miners. Their growth has raised concerns about safety standards, regulatory oversight and environmental protection.

item.title: [BBC World] Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo dies age 80
item.description:
Image source, EPAImage caption,
Mexican prison police secured the hospital where Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo was admitted earlier this weekByWill GrantBBC's Mexico, Central America and Cuba correspondent, Reporting fromMexico CityPublished48 minutes ago
Notorious Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo has died in hospital aged 80.
Félix Gallardo was widely considered one of the biggest drug smugglers in history and is credited with building an alliance between criminal groups in Colombia and his own Mexican cartel.
Known as The Godfather or the 'Boss of Bosses', Félix Gallardo was the head of the all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel, which reigned over Mexican drug trafficking at the height of the cocaine boom of the 1980s.
At the time, it created a new modus operandi in the illegal drug trade which endures to this day. He had been in state custody since 1989.
The name Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's.
He led the organisation which revolutionised drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly Escobar's Medellín Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States.
At one point an estimated 80% of all cocaine that entered the US came from the Medellín Cartel. Félix Gallardo and his organisation played a major role in smuggling it in.
At its height, the Guadalajara Cartel under Félix Gallardo influenced Mexican politics and law enforcement, controlling entire police networks and state governorships.
How one DEA killing began a brutal war
In 1985, the net started to tighten around the leaders of the cartel following the torture and murder of a DEA agent, Enrique 'Kiki' Camarena.

item.title: [NPR News] Far from home. Voyager 1 is now farther than anything man has sent into space
item.description:
News
Far from home. Voyager 1 is now farther than anything man has sent into space
November 15, 20265:41 PM ET
By
Ava Pukatch
This illustration provided by NASA depicts Voyager 1.
AP/NASA
hide caption
toggle caption i
AP/NASA
NASA's Voyager 1 has traveled farther than anything else that humans have launched into space. On Wednesday, it's set to reach a new milestone: reaching a distance that is one-light day away from Earth.
NASA is celebrating the occasion with the "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day." Calling it a symbolic celebration, NASA is asking the public on Tuesday night to send Voyager's call sign V-G-R into the sky in morse code. Use a flashlight, phone light or anything that can blink a sequence.
If you want to take part:
V - Three quick flashes, one long flash G - Two long flashes, one quick flash R - One quick flash, one long flash, one quick flash
What exactly is a light-day?
A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, or more than 16 billion miles.
This NASA spacecraft has traveled for nearly 50 years, launching Sept. 5, 1977.
Over the course of its mission, Voyager 1 has conducted flybys of Jupiter and Saturn. In 1979, it discovered a faint ring system on Jupiter. In 1980, the spacecraft took detailed photos of Saturn's rings and moons. ...

item.title: [BBC World] Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley as well as the political establishmentByDearbail Jordan, Business reporter and Lily Jamali, North America Technology correspondent, Reporting fromPalo Alto, CAPublished15 November 2026
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".
Also on Sunday, US Congressman John Moolenaar said that Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Select Committee on China, which he chairs, as well as the House Foreign Affairs and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.
The committee heads had threatened to issue subpoenas to Huang if he did not comply with their requests to testify.
Moolenaar told CBS, BBC's US partner, that none were ultimately issued. Huang's testimony is expected to take place behind close doors, with the dates still being finalised.

item.title: [NYT World] Jordan Sentences 3 to Death Over Greek Orthodox Church Attack
item.description:
AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENT
A military-run court in Jordan sentenced three men to death on Sunday after they were convicted in connection with an attack at a church last month that killed nine people, the Jordanian Armed Forces said in a statement.
The shooting at a Greek Orthodox church, which also wounded about three dozen people, was one of the deadliest militant attacks in the country in years, and King Abdullah II vowed that it would be met with “the harshest retaliation.”
The three men were sentenced after being convicted of violating antiterrorism laws, according to the Jordanian military. They were found guilty of carrying out deadly terrorist acts, possessing weapons and ammunition with the intent to commit terrorism, and promoting the ideas of a terrorist group.
That group was not named in the armed forces statement.
The sentences are subject to appeal, the military statement noted.
The three men were arrested in late October in Jordan after a shootout with security forces during a predawn raid on their hide-out in an abandoned house in the southern province of Karak, where the church attack took place. Karak is home to a sizable Christian community.
King Abdullah praised the arrests on social media. “No proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated,” he wrote.
Jordanian officials have not said what motivated the shooting at the church. Shortly afterward, Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said it was “the result of terrorist takfiri ideology,” using an Arabic phrase that often describes Islamist extremists who declare other Muslims heretics.
The sentencing on Sunday came a weeks after Jordan retaliated for the church attack with deadly airstrikes on Islamic State targets in southern Syria, a Jordanian government spokesman said at the time. The Jordanian military said it had been “targeting hide-outs of terrorist organizations,” without naming any specific group.

item.title: [ABC News World] Pope crosses Peru in finale of trip home to visit flock high in Andes, deep in Amazon
item.description:
Pope crosses Peru in finale of trip home to visit flock high in Andes, deep in Amazon
Pope Leo XIV is demanding justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the AmazonByNICOLE WINFIELD Associated Press, ASTRID SUAREZ Associated Press, MAURICIO SAVARESE Associated Press, and The Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 6:53 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
PUCALLPA, Peru -- From deep in the Peruvian rainforest, Pope Leo XIV on Sunday demanded justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon and fully backed efforts by Indigenous peoples to stop their lands from being ravaged by logging and illegal exploitation.
On the penultimate day of his South American odyssey, Leo traveled to the northeastern Peruvian Amazon city of Pucallpa and channelled one of Pope Francis’ core teachings that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God’s creation.
“The cry of the earth and the cry of the poor are inseparable,” Leo told Indigenous representatives and missionaries gathered along the Ucayali River.
He said he came to Pucallpa to support them in their search for justice and peace and referred to what environmental groups estimate have been 57 murders of environmental defenders between 2010-2024.
“The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice,” Leo said to applause from the crowd.
In addition to the decades-long problem of deforestation, illegal gold mining has become an increasingly lucrative business in the Amazon, devastating forests and polluting rivers. Miners use makeshift suction dredges and mercury, a toxic metal, to extract gold.
Raphael Hoetmer, Western Amazon program director at Amazon Watch, said wars and conflicts around the world have contributed to driving up the price of gold, increasing demand that in turn is resulting in more extraction from the Amazon.
“It’s causing pollution, health issues, and environmental degradation,” he said.

"We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said.

The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.
Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back".

item.title: [CBS News World] Megaspeed says Alice Huang left company in 2025, denies wrongdoing
item.description:
The Singapore-based company at the center of the scandal that brought down Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said Sunday that suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang left the company in 2025. It also denied any wrongdoing, saying it "conducts legitimate and lawful business."
In a statement to CBS News, Megaspeed International said Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, left the company in August 2025 and has no current role. It did not comment on the allegations that Alice Huang is a suspected Chinese spy.
"Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," the company's statement said.
Alice Huang was an executive at Megaspeed and is the woman with whom Jensen Huang was having an affair. She is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security, which China denies. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO last week.
U.S. investigators say Alice Huang used industry contacts and a series of shell companies to access 240,000 chips banned for export into China.
A screengrab from CTI video footage shows a woman identified by Reuters as Alice Huang attending a dinner with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, in black, at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan, May 22, 2025.
CTI via Reuters TV
In the past three years, Megaspeed has been one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and advanced hardware, The New York Times first reported.
Now the company, which began as an offshoot of a China-based gaming firm and grew into a juggernaut by gaining access to the Nvidia chips, is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling Nvidia's restricted AI computer chips into China.

Gen. Abdullah Saberi, an Iranian commander, stepped out for a jog early one morning in an upscale diplomatic quarter of Syria’s capital. Israeli intelligence officers waited nearby. Posing as movers, they had slipped past the neighborhood’s security checkpoints.
As he headed for a nearby park, General Saberi passed two men who carried an oversize refrigerator box. In a flash, the men restrained the general, drugged him, threw the box over his head, shoved him into a white van and left as if nothing had happened.
He was whisked to Israel for interrogation, according to numerous officials in the Middle East, including senior Iranian officials close to General Saberi and a Syrian official who reviewed video of the September 2021 kidnapping.
As a veteran of Iran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, General Saberi knew many secrets. But his interrogators were interested in only one.
What did he know about Ron Arad?
Mr. Arad, an Israeli airman, vanished decades ago, and the Israeli military says he is the only service member classified as missing in action. SEC. SEAN DUFFY: So we have some delays in the airspace right now, but as we look to the end of the day and into tomorrow, we should be running at full capacity. item.description:
Thousands run Cuba’s Marabana marathon as many protest US sanctions
Thousands of people have run in Cuba’s Marabana marathon, using the event to protest U.S. economic sanctionsByANDREA RODRIGUEZ Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 10:56 AM
Share
HAVANA -- Thousands of people ran Sunday in Cuba’s most important international marathon, with some using the race to protest U.S. economic sanctions against the island.
The Marabana marathon, held every November to commemorate the founding of Havana, took runners along city's iconic streets and landmarks, such as the Paseo del Prado and the Capitol building. Many wore signs expressing solidarity with Cuba.
“Cuba is not a threat; the blockade is,” read the signs that many of the 3,000 participants wore on their backs.
The U.S. embargo against Cuba was first imposed in 1960, after Fidel Castro led a revolution that toppled dictator Fulgencio Batista and nationalized properties belonging to U.S. citizens and corporations. As a result, the Caribbean country has endured decades of economic and financial troubles and is now being pushed to a breaking point after U.S. President Donald Trump announced in late January that he would impose tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to Cuba.
The warning has effectively cut off fuel to the island, leading to widespread power outages that disrupt water supplies and internet and telephone services.
“The blockade is suffocating the Cuban people," Yuraldi Cava, a 58-year-old state employee, said while running. “We are going to win this fight.”
Mayté Vigoa, Havana’s provincial government coordinator for sports, said the city had to make a major effort to hold the international race because of the island’s precarious economic conditions. She confirmed that the sportswear brand Adidas, a longtime sponsor of the competition, did not provide support this year.

To the scientists and wardens of Banff National Park he is grizzly bear 122. But to everyone who lives in or near Canada’s oldest national park, and many of its 4.5 million annual visitors, he is the Boss.
He has been struck by a freight train without apparent ill effect. He has shrugged off being hit by cars. Scientists have confirmed that he killed and snacked on a black bear at least once, and he is believed to have fathered many, if not most, of the bears in his 2,000-square-kilometer territory.
Most of all, the Boss has become Canada’s 700-pound celebrity bear king. When he strolls along the Trans-Canada Highway looking for dandelions, “bear jams” swiftly follow. His battles with a rival bear known as Split Lip are legendary. (He caused the split lip.) His annual awakening from hibernation, usually in March, is reported by news outlets across Alberta.
Galleries in Banff and neighboring Canmore ship giant photos of him worldwide. His image appears on fridge magnets, T-shirts and tote bags. A local restaurant is named for him, its main dining room dominated by a scrap metal sculpture of the bear.Image

Czechs gather in big numbers to reject government's plan to overhaul funding of public media
Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague against a government plan to overhaul funding for public broadcastersByKAREL JANICEK ASSOCIATION PRESS Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 10:22 AM
Share
PRAGUE -- Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague on Sunday against a plan by the government of Czech billionaire Andrej Babiš to overhaul funding for public broadcasters that many say will erode media independence and democracy.
The massive protest took place at the capital's Letná Park, where huge crowds gathered during the 1989 Velvet Revolution, which ended more than 40 years of communist rule in the country.
The rally, just two days before the anniversary of the 1989 protests, drew an estimated 350,000 people, said Mikuláš Minář, the lead organizer from the Million Moments for Democracy group. They demanded that the government withdraw its plan and expressed concern that Babiš and his coalition partners pose a threat to democracy.
“We do witness here something extraordinary today,” Minář said.
Under the plan, the country’s public radio and television broadcasters would be financed from the state budget, replacing the existing system of regular fees paid by individuals, households and businesses. The broadcasters would receive about 15% less money than they do now, which could lead to layoffs, limited production and program cancellations.
Critics say the overhaul would give the three-party coalition the means to take control of the media, similar to what populist governments did in Slovakia under Prime Minister Robert Fico and in Hungary, before former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April.
“We refuse the Slovak scenario,” one protest banner read. “Hands off the media,” said another.

Tussle for influence as trade, tech and regional security to take centre stage in China, Philippines and Cambodia meetings
World leaders will fly in to Asia for back-to-back high-level summits this week against the backdrop of the tussle for influence between the superpowers China and the US.
Beijing will have the home advantage when it welcomes Donald Trump to its southern technology hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting. It starts two weeks after the US leader lost midterm elections.
The summit also comes after an awkward-at-best revelation that the head of Nvidia, the US chipmaker that for a long time was the world’s most valuable company, was having an affair with a woman US intelligence suspects was a Chinese spy.
Apec represents more than 60% of global GDP and has primarily promoted free trade and multilateralism. This year’s meeting could be defined, however, by the confirmed trilateral meeting between Trump, the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.
The three-way meeting has been likened to a modern-day Yalta, when in 1945 then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to carve up Europe after the second world war. However, analysts say a “Yalta 2.0” that issues edicts on Ukraine and Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, is among those who have expressed concern that the world will witness a Yalta 2.0 moment if Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet trilaterally, as expected, on the sidelines of the Apec summit in China next week.
It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse.
Putin has long proposed this re-enactment of the greatest wartime summit, held in February 1945 at Joseph Stalin’s insistence in a rundown Tsarist resort on the south coast of Crimea alongside Franklin D Roosevelt and Winston Churchill.
Trump has cast himself in the role of the enthusiastic guest while Xi acts the bashful host, ever reluctant to embrace the status of a traditional global superpower.
No one quite knows what will happen if the three men meet or even if China will allow more than a stiff protocol-driven exchange of statements. China is already trying to push nuclear disarmament off the agenda.

The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.
Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.
The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”
She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.
“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”

Watch: Chris Cash says counter-terror officers entered his bedroom and arrested himByJoe Pike, politics investigations correspondent and Phil Kemp, politics reporterPublished11 November 2026
A British man who was charged with spying for China has told the BBC he was a "convenient fall guy" for UK police and security services who wanted to put espionage threats by foreign states "on the map".
Chris Cash, a former parliamentary researcher, has shared more than 6,000 messages with us revealing how a Chinese official sought information about sensitive political matters in the UK - including the 2022 Tory leadership battle to decide the next prime minister.
The messages show how Cash's friend in China, Chris Berry - with whom he had been sharing information - dramatically described a "secret" meeting between Berry and a high-ranking Chinese official.
Berry said he had been told that China was concerned about how a British MP it had sanctioned might be promoted to a cabinet role.
The messages also reveal how Cash used his friend as a reference during vetting for a parliamentary pass - which was approved.
Like Cash, Berry was also charged with espionage. The two men consistently maintained their innocence.
In Cash's first interview since his acquittal, which sparked a political row over the government's failure to designate China as a "threat", he says he would "never do anything" to harm UK national security.
But he admits he was "unprofessional and naive" to send "gossiping" texts to his friend, whom he met in 2018 when they both taught English in a school in China.
Although the trove of messages shows him discussing sensitive topics, there is no evidence in them that Cash was paid by, or sympathetic to, the Chinese Communist Party.

Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo
Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.
The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.
An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said.
The health ministry gave the casualty toll, adding more than 70 of the injured were discharged after receiving treatment.
Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways.
Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances.
Gamal said he saw about 80 of the injured being taken by ambulances to hospital. Some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and died, he said.
